title: TypeScript — From JavaScript to Safe Contracts
description: Migrate working JavaScript into explicit, maintainable contracts and understand where compile-time safety ends.

lessons.title: Type Inference and Annotations
lessons.why: Here’s the simple reason this matters: Type inference lets TypeScript discover useful types from values and control flow so you do not have to annotate everything manually. In this course, we connect it directly to the contracts that make TaskFlow code safer before it reaches runtime, so you can see where the idea lives in a real project instead of memorizing a definition.
objectives: Explain Type Inference and Annotations in terms of inputs, owner, outputs, and failure modes.
Implement Type Inference and Annotations incrementally and predict observable evidence before execution.
Diagnose a controlled Type Inference and Annotations failure from evidence.
Apply Type Inference and Annotations to a new TaskFlow requirement without copying the reference implementation.
prerequisites: Complete the previous lesson in TypeScript — From JavaScript to Safe Contracts or demonstrate equivalent skill.
Start from a healthy project/checkpoint.
mentalModel: Start with the plain-English idea. Type inference lets TypeScript discover useful types from values and control flow so you do not have to annotate everything manually.

Now place it in TaskFlow. This lesson belongs to the contracts that make TaskFlow code safer before it reaches runtime. Ask four questions while you work: what enters this boundary, who owns the decision, what dependency does it use, and what evidence proves the result?

Keep the change small. Predict what you should see before you run anything, then compare the prediction with the real terminal, browser, HTTP, database, test, container, or CI evidence. If they differ, debug the first mismatch instead of editing several places at random.

The goal is not to remember the exact snippet below. The goal is to be able to explain Type Inference and Annotations in your own words, rebuild the core behavior, and adapt it when the requirement changes.
